prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: Link Inventory Audit — Q1 2025 (language en).
Grid: 4 columns × 7 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Per-column content facts (content px at 13px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Page title" · longest unbreakable word 88px · one-line width 282px
  col 2: header "URL" · longest unbreakable word 287px · one-line width 744px
  col 3: header "Last checked" · longest unbreakable word 54px · one-line width 84px
  col 4: header "Status code" · longest unbreakable word 42px · one-line width 76px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 767px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 766px.
Fixed: content, font, 13px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Your understanding so far: {"purpose":"Audit a set of links by identifying each page and URL alongside its most recent check and resulting status code.","reading":"Readers scan page titles to find an entry, follow the row to its URL, and compare check dates and status codes across entries. Wrapped titles and URLs can share the same row height, provided each row remains easy to follow.","groups":["Page title and URL identify the same destination; the title supports scanning while the URL gives the precise address.","Last checked and Status code describe the result of the audit and should remain compact and easy to compare vertically."],"keep_intact":["Dates and status codes","Unbreakable URL segments","Individual words in page titles and column headers"],"may_wrap":["Page titles at natural word boundaries","URLs at available break opportunities"]}

The first image is the one-line content overview. The other images are real browser renders of your current designs:
Design r1A: widths [185, 379, 105, 97] · table 767×414px · row heights [33, 73, 73, 53, 53, 53, 73] · column headers wrapped 0/4 · tallest cell 3 lines · mid-word splits 0
Design r1B: widths [145, 419, 105, 97] · table 767×475px · row heights [33, 73, 94, 73, 73, 53, 73] · column headers wrapped 0/4 · tallest cell 4 lines · mid-word splits 0
Design r1C: widths [205, 359, 105, 97] · table 767×434px · row heights [33, 73, 73, 53, 53, 73, 73] · column headers wrapped 0/4 · tallest cell 3 lines · mid-word splits 0

Look carefully at each render as a whole and in detail. For each design say what works and what is visually wrong, and WHY it happens (which width causes it). Then propose up to 3 improved designs: refine the most promising, fix the problems you saw, and try a new idea if an important alternative is unexplored. If no design can be meaningfully improved, set "done": true and return no new designs.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"critique":[{"design":"name","good":"","problems":"","cause":""}],"done":false,"designs":[{"name":"short-name","widths":[int px],"change":"what you changed and why"}]}
